headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.29–2.65), indicating no statistically significant association between polyunsaturated fat (pufa) and renal cell carcinoma. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 95.59%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: Among polyunsaturated fatty acids, linoleic acid (OR = 0.5; 95% CI: 0.4-0.7; p-value for trend = 0.0001) and linolenic acid (OR = 0.7; 95% CI: 0.5-1.0; p-value for trend = 0.01) were inversely related to RCC.

sample_size.excerpt: We examined data from 84,063 eligible Japanese participants aged 45 to 74 years who responded to a validated food frequency questionnaire for Cohort I in 1995 and Cohort II in 1998. The participants were followed-up until 2013.

cases.excerpt: Among the 1,272,298 person-years of follow-up, 262 cases of newly diagnosed RCC were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: lowest quartile of fish, including shellfish, were (HR = 1.43; 95% CI, 0.98-2.07) and the individual marine n-3 PUFAs were (HR = 1.56; 95% CI, 1.07-2.28; Ptrend = 0.09) for eicosapentenoic acid, (HR = 1.81; 95% CI, 1.27-2.59; Ptrend = 0.01) for docosapentaenoic acid, and (HR = 1.56; 95% CI, 1.07-2.27; Ptrend = 0.09) for docosahexaenoic acid.
